overview: Peru is a country on the west coast of South America. Its capital and largest city is Lima. Peru was the centre of the Inca Empire, and its mountain city of Machu Picchu is one of the most famous archaeological sites in the world. Peru won independence from Spain in 1821. Spanish, Quechua and Aymara are official languages.

geography.text: Peru has three main regions: a narrow desert along the Pacific coast, the high Andes running through the middle, and the Amazon rainforest, which covers more than half the country, in the east. The Amazon river begins in the Peruvian Andes. Lake Titicaca, on the border with Bolivia, is often called the highest navigable lake in the world.

subsections.title: Climate
subsections.text: Dry desert on the coast, cold in the Andes and hot and wet in the Amazon.

subsections.title: Wildlife
subsections.text: Llamas, alpacas, Andean condors and the pink river dolphins of the Amazon.

history.text: Peru was home to Caral, part of the oldest known civilisation in the Americas, and later to the Nazca and the Inca, whose empire stretched along the Andes. Spanish conquerors led by Francisco Pizarro defeated the Inca in the 1530s, and Lima became the capital of Spanish South America. Peru declared independence in 1821.

events.title: Inca expansion
events.text: Pachacuti begins turning the Inca state into an empire.

events.title: Pizarro captures Atahualpa
events.text: Spanish conquerors seize the Inca emperor.

events.title: Independence
events.text: José de San Martín declares Peru independent.

events.title: War of the Pacific
events.text: Peru and Bolivia lose territory to Chile.

events.title: Machu Picchu
events.text: The Inca city is brought to world attention by the explorer Hiram Bingham.

government.text: Peru is a presidential republic. The President is elected every five years and cannot serve two terms in a row. Congress has one chamber. Peru has had many Presidents in recent years, several of whom were removed by Congress or prosecuted for corruption.

economy.text: Peru is one of the world's largest producers of copper, silver, gold and zinc. It also exports fish meal, avocados, blueberries and grapes. Tourism, especially to Machu Picchu, is important.

culture.text: Peru was the heart of the Inca Empire, and Quechua is still spoken by millions. Its food is one of the most celebrated in the world, with dishes such as ceviche, raw fish 'cooked' in lime juice. Peru has thousands of potato varieties.

items.title: Machu Picchu
items.text: An Inca city high in the Andes, built in the 1400s.

items.title: Ceviche
items.text: A national dish listed by UNESCO in 2023.

items.title: Nazca Lines
items.text: Giant drawings in the desert, best seen from the air.

subsections.title: Food
subsections.text: Ceviche, lomo saltado (stir-fried beef) and thousands of kinds of potato.

subsections.title: Music and arts
subsections.text: Andean weaving and music with pan pipes; Lima's restaurants are among the best in the world.

subsections.title: Traditions and festivals
subsections.text: Inti Raymi, the Inca festival of the Sun, is held in Cusco every June.

sport.text: Football is the most popular sport; Peru won the Copa América in 1939 and 1975. Women's volleyball won Olympic silver in 1988. Surfer Sofía Mulánovich became world champion in 2004.

items.text: Women's volleyball Olympic silver in Seoul.

items.title: Sofía Mulánovich
items.text: The first South American world surfing champion.
Lima hosted the Pan American Games.
